item.title: I stripped the distractions out of Android Auto, and I like it so much more now
item.itunes:title: I stripped the distractions out of Android Auto, and I like it so much more now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I use Android Auto almost every time I get behind the wheel, so even small annoyances start to stand out over time. What bothered me most wasn't navigation or music, but how much unnecessary stuff kept appearing on the screen and demanding attention.

I eventually started switching off the features I could live without, mostly to see whether I would miss them. I didn't. Android Auto now feels cleaner, calmer, and much easier to glance at while driving.

I cleaned up the Android Auto launcher

My launcher was way too crowded

My Android Auto launcher had slowly turned into a dumping ground. By default, it shows all the compatible apps in the dashboard. That meant I had several messaging apps, multiple music streaming services like Spotify and Amazon Music, and even local players like Musicolet and Poweramp that I had installed mainly for testing.

On top of that, Android Auto showed apps like Google News, Adobe Acrobat, and several others I had no reason to use while driving. I finally went into the Android Auto Settings on my Galaxy S25 Ultra, selected Customize launcher, and removed everything I didn't regularly use behind the wheel.

Now, my launcher is limited to a much smaller set of essentials, such as Messages, Google Maps, YouTube Music, Gemini Actions, and a few other shortcuts I actually need. It sounds like a minor cleanup, but it makes a major difference. I no longer have to scroll through rows of irrelevant icons to find what I want, and there is far less temptation to poke around the screen while driving. Everything important is right where I expect it.

I never take a long drive without changing these Android Auto settings

Tiny changes, smoother hours behind the wheel

By  Parth Shah

I removed unnecessary taskbar widgets

I stripped the taskbar back

The taskbar is another area where Android Auto has started to feel busier than I wanted. I had shortcuts and widgets sitting there that looked useful on paper, but I rarely touched them during an actual drive. They took up space and added more information to an interface that should be as simple as possible.

So I trimmed the taskbar down and kept only the apps I use. I don't need every media shortcut, suggested action, or extra widget visible all the time. I mainly rely on the default Android Auto home, where I can access Maps, Music, and other details with a single tap. I headed into Android Auto's Settings and disabled Taskbar Widgets from the Display menu. There is less visual noise around the navigation screen, fewer things looking to get my attention, and Android Auto now feels much more purpose-built for driving.

I disabled message chimes

I silenced the constant message pings

Message chimes were one of those small Android Auto features that became annoying over time. Every incoming message interrupted the cabin with a sound, even when I had no intention of checking or replying.

On a busy day, those alerts could pile up quickly and turn an otherwise calm drive into a constant stream of interruptions. I eventually disabled message chimes altogether. I still get notifications on the Android Auto screen, so I am not completely cut off, but there is no sound demanding my attention every few minutes.

If something is important, I can deal with it using Gemini (more on that in a minute) or wait until I stop the car. It is another tiny change, but it has made my drives noticeably quieter. I still stay reachable when needed, without every group chat or casual message coming in my way. To turn the feature off, go to Settings > Connected Devices > Connection Preferences > Android Auto > Messaging > turn off Show Message Chime.

I rely more on Gemini voice controls now

Voice controls replaced most screen taps

Once I stripped away most distractions, I started touching the Android Auto screen a lot less. Instead, I rely heavily on Gemini. A press of the voice button on my steering wheel is usually all it takes to get something done without taking my eyes off the road.

I can start a call, send my ETA to someone through Messages or WhatsApp, ask for directions, play a specific song on YouTube Music (even with a vague description), or find a nearby fuel station. But I also use it for things that go beyond the usual driving commands.

I can ask Gemini to pull up information from my meeting notes, create a new task or reminder, add something to a list, and handle other small things that would normally require reaching for my phone. That has become my preferred way to use Android Auto. I keep the interface simple and let my voice handle most of the work.

I removed everything I didn't need

Android Auto is at its best when it stays out of the way. I don't need every compatible app, widget, or shortcut competing for space on the dashboard. I still have everything I actually need, including navigation, music, calls, messages, and Gemini, but there is far less visual and audible clutter around them. For me, the simpler setup is better.

I turned an old phone into a permanent Android Auto device, and my main phone never connects to the car anymore

My Pixel 8 Pro is now my dedicated Android Auto device.

3
By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: I turned Obsidian into a personal command center with these 6 free plugins
item.itunes:title: I turned Obsidian into a personal command center with these 6 free plugins
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve used plenty of productivity apps, but I keep coming back to Obsidian because I can customize it so much. On its own, it’s a solid place to store notes, but the right plugins can take it much further. What started as a simple note-taking setup can become a powerful workspace without adding another subscription to my list. The best part is that I can choose the features I actually need instead of paying for a bundle of tools I might never use. Here are six Obsidian plugins that make it feel like an app I’d happily pay for.

Excalidraw

A whiteboard hiding inside Obsidian

I’ve always found it easier to understand some ideas when I can see them than when I read about them. That’s where Excalidraw comes in. It brings a freehand drawing canvas into Obsidian, letting me sketch ideas, create flowcharts, and map out concepts without switching to another app. I like its hand-drawn look because it feels more like working through an idea on paper than using a complicated diagramming tool.

I can also embed my drawings in notes and connect them to the rest of my vault. I find it especially useful when planning a project, breaking down a complex topic, or figuring out how different pieces fit together. It makes Obsidian a much better space for visual thinking.

Dataview

Build dynamic dashboards from your notes

My Obsidian vault quickly became a mess of notes, and finding the right information started taking more time than it should. Dataview changed that for me. It lets me pull information from across my vault and display it in useful tables, lists, and task views. I can filter notes by tags, dates, folders, and custom properties instead of searching through everything manually.

What I like most is that these views update automatically as I add or change notes. I can create a list of my blog ideas, track their status, or see recently updated notes on a single page. It makes my existing notes far more useful without forcing me to reorganize my entire vault.

Templater

Make every new note effortless to create

I got tired of creating the same note structure every time I started something new. Templater solved that problem by letting me create templates with dynamic content instead of relying on static text. I can automatically insert dates, file names, and other details whenever I create a note. I can also use JavaScript to build more advanced templates that adapt to what I need.

I can set up a meeting notes template with the date and standard headings already filled in, or create a research note with predefined sections. What I like most is how much repetitive work it removes from my routine. Once I set up a template, I can reuse it whenever I need it without starting from scratch.

I gave Claude read access to my Obsidian vault, and it found connections I'd forgotten I made

Years of notes were hiding valuable insights in my Obsidian vault until Claude connected them in ways I never expected.

By  Yash Patel

Tasks

Take your everyday task management further

I used to think the regular checkboxes in Obsidian were enough for managing my to-do list, but they started feeling limited as my workload grew. The Tasks plugin adds the features I was missing, including due dates, priorities, recurring tasks, and filters. I can assign a deadline to a task inside a note and still find it later through a central task list. I also like being able to create custom views for overdue tasks, upcoming deadlines, or tasks with a particular priority.

This saves me from moving everything into a separate task management app just to stay organized. Tasks makes Obsidian much more useful for managing everyday responsibilities without separating my tasks from the notes where they belong.

Kanban

Bring your projects to life visually

I often struggle to see how a project is progressing when everything is buried in a long list of notes. The Kanban plugin gives me a simple visual board where I can organize work into columns and move cards between them as things progress. I can create columns such as Ideas, In Progress, and Completed, then move each task to the right stage with a quick drag-and-drop.

What I like is that the board feels lightweight and easy to manage without the extra features of a full project management tool. I can also link cards to my existing notes for more details. For tracking personal projects or managing a simple workflow, it makes Obsidian feel much more practical.

Advance Tables

Cleaner tables with fewer keystrokes

I didn't realize how much time I wasted fixing Markdown tables until I started working with larger ones. Advanced Tables makes the whole process easier by handling the formatting for me. I can move between cells using the keyboard, add new rows, and keep columns aligned without manually adjusting the Markdown syntax. I find this especially helpful when putting together software comparisons, research findings, or lists of tools with several features to compare.

Formula support is another useful addition when I need to run simple calculations inside a table. What I appreciate most is that I can focus on the information instead of fighting with formatting. It's a small improvement, but one that makes working with structured data in Obsidian much more comfortable.

I stopped using Obsidian like a notes app, and started using it like a database

When retrieval is the bottleneck, build a system.

5
By  Yash Patel

Obsidian isn't just a note-taking app anymore

What makes Obsidian special is how easily I can shape it around the way I work. These plugins add capabilities that I'd otherwise look for in separate apps, without forcing me into someone else's workflow. I don't need every plugin or a complicated setup to get the most out of it. I just need the right tools for my daily needs. And that's what makes Obsidian feel like an app I'd happily pay for.

item.title: I tried an open-source Obsidian alternative, and it’s the first AI note app I actually trust
item.itunes:title: I tried an open-source Obsidian alternative, and it’s the first AI note app I actually trust
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every note-taking app has spent the last couple of years bolting on AI, and it tends to look the same in all of them: a chat box that can summarize what you're working on and not much else. And the apps that go a little further with more comprehensive AI features usually do it by keeping your notes in their cloud database. This is not a very easy sell for an Obsidian user who specifically uses the app to keep their work local.

Then an open-source editor showed up in June, called OpenKnowledge, and it's built on the idea that the AI tools you already pay for should be able to work inside your notes directly, and locally.

What OpenKnowledge actually is

It works like an Obsidian vault, just built with a second user in mind

OpenKnowledge comes from Inkeep, an AI agent company, and it's a free, open-source markdown editor that's built for you and your AI tools to work on the same documents together. You can point it at any folder on your drive, so obviously one of the first things I tried was my Obsidian vault. Everything showed up exactly as I'd left it, even the non-markdown files, and their links were all still intact.

There's no database behind your files here. Notes are plain .md files in a regular folder, same as a vault, which explains why when I went hunting for an export button, I couldn't find any - instead, it appears any note you create in the OpenKnowledge app automatically populates in your chosen folder. It keeps its own settings in a hidden .ok folder and ignores Obsidian's settings folder, and the docs say it won't move or rename your notes.

item.title: The $1,049 Steam Machine isn't a bad deal — I just priced one out and proved it to myself
item.itunes:title: The $1,049 Steam Machine isn't a bad deal — I just priced one out and proved it to myself
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
We'd all been waiting avidly to hear Valve reveal the price for the Steam Machine, much like millions of gamers around the world. So when I first saw the $1,049 price tag attached to the "PC console," my immediate reaction was that I could build something better for less. I've built enough PCs to know that a four-digit price tag can go pretty far, especially when I get to pick every component myself. As such, Valve's little box looked like exactly the sort of prebuilt that I'd confidently tell someone to avoid.

And yet, things got a lot more interesting when I started pricing out an equivalent machine. The closer I got to replicating what Valve is actually selling, the less convincing my original argument became. I still think $1,049 sounds expensive, but now, I'm no longer sure it's the bad deal I initially thought it was.

Despite its price, Valve reportedly sells up to 15,000 Steam Machines a week

A pretty good start.

7
By  Simon Batt

I tried to build the Steam Machine myself

The component list looks deceptively simple

The Steam Machine boasts a semi-custom CPU from AMD, so there's no retail chip exactly like it. What comes closest to its Zen 4 6-core 12-thread processor, however, is the Ryzen 5 7600, with the Radeon RX 7600 being the closest GPU equivalent to the Steam Machine's RDNA 3 28CU, 8GB VRAM graphics processor. It isn't a perfect one-to-one match, but it does put us in the right architecture and performance territory.

Pairing it with a B650 motherboard is the obvious next step, and matching the Steam Machine's 16GB of RAM with a 16GB DDR5-6000 kit of my own was a no-brainer. Since the $1,049 model of the Steam Machine ships with 512GB of NVMe storage, I decided to stick with the same amount instead of reaching for a 1TB SSD — SSD prices in 2026 are no joke, after all. Now, none of these components are particularly exotic, but that's precisely the point.

The power supply was the annoying part, and getting a compact case is as easy as finding the first decent $60 cabinet at the local store. This part of the build did, however, introduce dimensional constraints instead of financial ones, and it was all before I even started charging myself for assembling it.

Clearly, even the basic parts to build a PC as close as possible to the Steam Machine were ballooning my budget past the GabeCube's $1,049 price tag. The biggest culprits, of course, were the RAM and the SSD, which used to be available earlier at $60 each (better times), but now demand a RAMflation premium. I couldn't be too mad, though, since it's the exact environment that forced Valve to release the Steam Machine with a four-figure price tag.

Not only was my "closest equivalent" almost a full hundred dollars over the Steam Machine's retail price, but it also wasn't quite the slam dunk I'd expected it to be. Not a single component on this PC could wildly outperform its Steam Machine equivalent, after all.

16GB of RAM is still perfectly usable in 2026, and I'm tired of pretending it isn't

It's not the mistake everyone says it is

5
By  Samarveer Singh

The Steam Machine sells peace of mind, too

One box, one brand, and considerably less troubleshooting

There's a reason consoles continue to sell millions of units despite gaming PCs offering better performance per dollar. A PS5 or Xbox is one complete product, with one manufacturer responsible for making the entire experience work. I've talked about how the Steam Machine promises that same convenience, and I think that's considerably more valuable than its spec sheet lets on.

Assembling a PC always comes with separate component warranties to juggle with, motherboard quirks, and driver issues you can't ever see coming. When something goes wrong, figuring out whether the culprit is your GPU, power supply, or some obscure software conflict becomes your unpaid second job.

On the other hand, with Valve's machine, there's one company to buy from, one brand to contact when trouble strikes, and a single piece of hardware designed to work as a cohesive product.

Plus, there's Steam itself — Valve has spent decades building goodwill with PC gamers through its storefront, ecosystem, and features that make buying and playing games remarkably painless. Sure, that doesn't somehow automatically justify the $1,049 price tag, but it does count for something. With the Steam Machine, you're buying a fully established ecosystem instead of picking components off a shelf and hoping they all work as seamlessly as Valve's hardware.

The Steam Machine is actually a Mac mini competitor, but not in the way you think

Valve is doing what Apple perfected

By  Samarveer Singh

I still wouldn't tell every PC gamer to buy the Steam Machine

The best value depends on what you're actually paying for

The Steam Machine becomes an incredibly hard sell if you already own a gaming PC. For anyone like myself who has already paid for the pricey components that make a desktop tick, spending another $1,049 for a compact system running SteamOS makes little sense, unless you specifically want a dedicated living-room machine. There's no reason to spend a thousand dollars when you can simply spend chump change on getting Ethernet into your TV and self-host your own PC's entire gaming library through Moonlight and Apollo.

There's also the fact that building your own PC gives you control that Valve simply can't hand over. The ability to upgrade individual components, reuse hardware you already own, and spend more of your budget on performance is something the Steam Machine doesn't provide at all. If squeezing every last frame out of your money is the objective, a DIY build remains the more sensible route.

But for someone who wants PC gaming without the assembly, troubleshooting, and endless component comparisons, the equation changes. The Steam Machine offers a console-like experience without abandoning the Steam library, and that convenience has genuine value. I wouldn't, in good conscience, call the Steam Machine an outright bargain, but I wouldn't dismiss it as overpriced, either.

Sometimes, convenience is worth paying for

I've always believed that building a PC should be about getting exactly what you want out of your hardware, not blindly chasing the cheapest way to play games. And yet, having spent several weekends tinkering and troubleshooting when something inevitably went wrong, I can also see why someone might want to skip it all. The Steam Machine challenges the assumption that every gaming device needs to justify itself through raw performance per dollar. I still prefer having control over my hardware, and I suspect plenty of PC enthusiasts will agree. But that doesn't change the fact that the Steam Machine delivers a dependable, genuinely console-like experience at its price, which means that not every dollar needs to go toward another frame per second.

As such, Valve's little box looked like exactly the sort of prebuilt that I'd confidently tell someone to avoid.

And yet, things got a lot more interesting when I started pricing out an equivalent machine. The closer I got to replicating what Valve is actually selling, the less convincing my original argument became. I still think $1,049 sounds expensive, but now, I'm no longer sure it's the bad deal I initially thought it was.

A pretty good start.

item.title: I spent 20 minutes turning my ISP router into a plain modem, and my network finally stabilized
item.itunes:title: I spent 20 minutes turning my ISP router into a plain modem, and my network finally stabilized
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Everyone blames their ISP first. I did it for weeks, with speed tests at 2 a.m., long stares at the gateway Xfinity rents me, and eventually a second router bought on sale.

The speed tests always came back fast, around 918 Mbps, while my calls kept freezing for half a minute at a time. What actually fixed it was bridge mode, a setting that turns the gateway into a plain modem, and it took me 20 minutes.

The speed test kept saying I was wrong

Wired and Wi-Fi went down at the same moment

My setup was the one most people never touch. An Xfinity XB7 gateway sat on a living room shelf doing three jobs at once: modem, router, and Wi-Fi for 41 devices. Most are tiny things, like smart plugs and a thermostat that phones home every few minutes.

The dropouts never showed up in a speed test because they never lasted long enough. Everything would go dark for 15 to 40 seconds, then come back as if nothing had happened. So I started a log: a ping -t 1.1.1.1 window running on my desktop, plus a note on my phone whenever the TV showed its no-connection screen in the middle of Sunday football. Over seven days, I counted nine dropouts.

Wired and wireless dropped at the same moment every time, which ruled out the Wi-Fi. That left the line, the modem, or the router half of the gateway, and I couldn't tell them apart while they lived in the same box. Splitting them up is exactly why the fix worked.

My first fix made two routers argue

My new router snitched on my old one

I bought an ASUS TUF Gaming AX4200, a Wi-Fi 6 gaming router, plugged its WAN port into the gateway, and called it a night. ASUS's spec sheet lists a 2GHz quad-core processor and 512MB of RAM, which is plenty for a home full of smart plugs. Wi-Fi felt snappier straight away, and I went to bed feeling smug.

The smugness lasted until the next evening. I tried to open my Jellyfin server from my phone on cellular, and it just spun. I'd forwarded the port on the ASUS, and the ASUS was doing exactly what I'd asked. Nothing was getting to it.

The culprit was double NAT, which just means two routers are each rewriting addresses on the same trip out. The ASUS could open a door on its side, but the gateway kept its own door shut, so outside requests died at the first box.

You can check for it in about 10 seconds on Windows. Open Terminal and run tracert -d 1.1.1.1. My first hop was 192.168.50.1, the ASUS, and my second was 10.0.0.1, the gateway. Two private addresses in a row means two routers are translating. On a Mac, traceroute -n 1.1.1.1 shows the same thing. The ASUS had noticed too, since its DDNS page warned that the router seemed to be sitting behind another NAT. Caught in 4K by my own router.

I ran double NAT for two years without knowing it, and fixing it explained problems I'd blamed on everything else

A single setting undid two years of guesswork.

18
By  Samir Makwana

Bridge mode took 20 minutes, mostly finding a sticker

One warning box, then nothing broke

Xfinity's support page lays out the steps. You open the Admin Tool at 10.0.0.1, sign in as admin with the password from the sticker on the gateway, go to Gateway -> At a Glance, and click Enable next to Bridge Mode.

Here's where my 20 minutes actually went. Five of them were me on the floor with a phone flashlight, reading a sticker on a gateway wedged behind a speaker. A few more went to the Xfinity app, because newer gateways make you switch on Admin Tool access there before 10.0.0.1 will even load.

Then came the warning box, which says bridge mode will disable the gateway's router and turn off its private Wi-Fi. That's the whole point, so I clicked OK. The gateway restarted, the ASUS picked up a public address on its WAN status page, and tracert showed one private hop instead of two. My Jellyfin server answered from cellular on the first try, and I cheered in an empty room.

Two details caught me out. Only one Ethernet port on the gateway stays active in bridge mode, so the router has to be the only thing plugged into it. And bridge mode doesn't turn off the Xfinity WiFi Home Hotspot, the public network some gateways broadcast for other customers. That's a separate toggle in the app.

Then I ran the same log for another week.

Measure (7 days each)

Gateway as router

Gateway as modem + ASUS

Dropouts of 10+ seconds

9

Times I power-cycled something

4

Wired download, median of five tests

918 Mbps

936 Mbps

Wired ping to 1.1.1.1

14 ms

13 ms

Speed barely moved, which is the point. The 918 from that Tuesday became 936, and that's noise. What changed was the boring stuff. No dropouts, no power-cycling, and no calls frozen mid-sentence.

Bridge mode hands you a few new jobs

The gateway stops being Xfinity's problem

Bridge mode isn't free. With it on, the Xfinity app still handles your account, but it can't manage your network anymore. Xfinity's WiFi Extenders, the pods it offers for dead zones, stop working, and its CyberSecure add-on goes away too.

Everything those features did is now my job. Firmware updates, the firewall, guest Wi-Fi, and coverage in the back bedroom all live on the ASUS, and when something breaks, I start troubleshooting. I've logged into the router more this month than I logged into the gateway all last year.

It won't help everyone, either. An XDA colleague swapped an ISP router for their own on fiber and saw no change at all. If your gateway isn't dropping out, and you don't need port forwarding, it's probably fine. And if you change your mind, it's reversible: plug a PC into the gateway with a cable, open the Admin Tool, and set Bridge Mode back to Disable.

Check for double NAT before you call your ISP

A month in, the ping window on my desktop is the most boring thing I own. That Tuesday call had nothing to do with the line coming into my home, because Xfinity was delivering more than 900 Mbps the whole time. My gateway was just doing one job too many.

If your internet is fast but flaky, run tracert and count the private hops before you call anyone. I won't blame the ISP again, at least not until I've checked that first.

item.title: I ran this hidden Claude Code command on my setup, and apparently I've been giving it terrible instructions
item.itunes:title: I ran this hidden Claude Code command on my setup, and apparently I've been giving it terrible instructions
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I like to think of myself as fairly good at prompting AI tools. A huge chunk of my daily work involves interacting with these models directly, I regularly attend briefings where the people actually building them share advice on how to get the most out of them, and I spend a good chunk of time seeing how other people are using them.

Well, to put it quite simply: it turns out I overestimated myself. A hidden Claude Code command that I didn't even know existed was all it took to expose that the instructions I've been giving it are just... terrible.

There’s a built-in command for auditing your Claude Code setup

Buried in plain sight

Before I talk about what the prompt-audit bit does specifically, though, it's worth explaining /doctor itself. The command has is essentially Claude Code's built-in diagnostics tool, and Anthropic describes it as a way to diagnose and verify your Claude Code installation and settings.

prompt-audit takes that same diagnostic idea in a much more interesting direction. Instead of checking whether Claude Code itself is set up correctly, it turns its attention to the instructions you've built around it.

While I initially thought that you'd use prompt-audit to analyze the prompts you'd sent Claude during a specific session, that's not really what it's designed for. Instead, it looks at the more permanent layer of instructions surrounding your Claude Code setup — things like your CLAUDE.md files, skills, custom commands, rules, subagents, and other configuration that can influence how Claude behaves across a project.

Once I ran the command, Claude first worked out exactly what it needed to inspect. In my case, that meant eight skills I'd created myself, 17 synced Anthropic skills, and seven installed plugins. Rather than going through all of that one file at a time, it split the job up between multiple subagents while continuing to inspect the smaller files itself.

Claude gave each subagent an extremely specific brief of what to do and what not to do. For example, one agent was assigned my Docker and presentation-related skills. Claude told it that the files were strictly read-only, warned it not to execute any commands it encountered inside them, explicitly treated the files as data rather than instructions, specified Claude Opus 5.5 as the model the prompts should be evaluated against, and even pointed it toward the exact sections of Anthropic's prompt-audit methodology it should follow.

The output format was fairly structured too. Claude asked the agent to return exact file locations, short quotes showing the offending instruction, the type of problem, why it was obsolete, a confidence rating, and what should be done about it. For anything that warranted a change, the agent also had to produce a proper diff containing the proposed replacement.

In total, Claude found 75 issues, split evenly across three different buckets. Twenty-five of them were in skills I had created myself, another 25 were in synced Anthropic skills, and the remaining 25 came from third-party plugins I had installed.

My Claude Code instructions had accumulated a lot of baggage

Prompt debt is apparently very real

Anthropic's reasoning behind the need for the /doctor prompt-audit command is that prompts tend to accumulate baggage as time passes.

Think about it — with how frequently AI providers roll out new models, do you realistically pay heed to the instructions you've already written every single time you switch to a newer one? Do you analyze how you currently write prompts, keeping in mind the strengths and flaws of the model you're now using, and then go back to rewrite old instructions accordingly?

While I've subconsciously begun to do that because of the nature of my work, I do admittedly leave plenty of instructions untouched once I've written them. If something seems to be working, I don't usually stop and ask whether the model still needs the same level of hand-holding it did a few months ago.

Claude Code's real power comes from the tweaks nobody wants to talk about

Claude Code gets better when you stop chasing flashy workflows and start tightening the boring setup details.

5
By  Jeff Butts

That's exactly the kind of baggage prompt-audit is designed to catch. item.title: The Dell XPS 13 proves sub-$1,000 laptops don't require many compromises
item.itunes:title: The Dell XPS 13 proves sub-$1,000 laptops don't require many compromises
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Spend enough time reading laptop recommendations, and you'll notice a pattern: the top options always seem to sit just above whatever budget you set for yourself. That's what makes the Dell XPS 13 worth a closer look. At $699.99, it brings the design language, screen quality, and everyday usability of Dell's flagship line to a price that sits comfortably under $1,000, without feeling like corners cut to hit that number.

That's not to say it's the right laptop for everyone. Buyers who need a lot of ports or maximum multitasking headroom will find real trade-offs here. But for those shopping for a Windows 11 laptop under $1,000 who want something that looks and feels premium day-to-day, the XPS 13 is one of the strongest laptops currently on the market.

Credit: Intel/Microsoft

Why the XPS 13 stands out at this price

Dell XPS 13 (2026)

Intel Core 5 320
Display (Size, Resolution)
13.4-inch, Touch, 2.5K, 30-120Hz, 500 nits

The Dell XPS 13 pairs a thin aluminum chassis with a 13.4-inch touch display that runs at up to 120Hz, delivering a premium feel rarely found at this size. At 2.2 pounds and 12.7mm thick, it's the lightest XPS built so far, with Wi-Fi 7 and up to 17 hours of battery life to power a full day of everyday computing, from browsing and streaming to documents and video calls.

See at Dell

The XPS 13 weighs 2.2 pounds and measures 12.7mm thick, making it the thinnest and lightest XPS laptop Dell has built. Those numbers matter more than you might think, because a laptop this size disappears into a bag in a way that heavier 15-inch and 16-inch machines don't. It's built from CNC-milled aluminum rather than plastic, which is usually the first thing to give way on a budget laptop.

None of this is unique to expensive laptops anymore, but it's still uncommon to find it at this price point. Many sub-$1,000 Windows laptops ask buyers to choose between a nice screen and a nice chassis. The XPS 13 doesn't ask that question.

A display that's genuinely hard to beat at this price

Credit: Dell

The screen is where the XPS 13 really shines. It's a 13.4-inch 2560x1600 touch display running at up to 120Hz with variable refresh between 30 and 120Hz, 500 nits of brightness, 100 percent DCI-P3 color coverage, and support for Dolby Vision and DisplayHDR 400. It also has an anti-glare finish, which is a small detail but a genuinely useful one if you tend to work near a window or outdoors.

Put plainly, this is a display specification you'd typically expect to see on a laptop costing several hundred dollars more. The touch support and 120Hz refresh in particular are still missing from many competing laptops in this price bracket, where 60Hz non-touch panels remain common.

Performance for everyday computing

The XPS 13 launches with an Intel® Core™ 5 processor, with Intel® Core™ Ultra Series 3 processor configurations expected later in the year. This is a laptop built for everyday computing rather than heavy creative or gaming workloads: browsing, documents, video calls, streaming, and general multitasking. For that kind of use, it holds up well.

Memory is worth a look. The XPS 13 ships with 8GB as standard, with a 16GB configuration available for $999.99. Anyone doing heavier multitasking, running lots of browser tabs alongside other applications, or planning to keep the laptop for several years should seriously consider stepping up to 16GB. At 8GB, it's fine for lighter use, but not something to overlook during configuration.

Storage and Wi-Fi are both solid for the price. The XPS 13 supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0, so connectivity isn't an area where anything has been trimmed back to hit the price point.

Battery life that suits a full day away from a charger

Dell rates the XPS 13 for up to 17 hours of video streaming, backed by a 52Wh battery. Real-world battery life depends heavily on what you're doing and how bright you run the screen, so treat that figure as a best-case number rather than a guarantee. Even so, it's a strong result for a laptop this thin, and it should comfortably cover a working day of typical use for most people.

How it stacks up against other laptops in this price range

Credit: Dell

The under-$1,000 segment of the Windows laptop market is crowded, and most of the competition falls into one of two camps: laptops that are design-light but heavy on ports, or laptops that look premium but cut into performance or screen quality to get there. The XPS 13 is unusual in that it doesn't really pick a side.

Compared with similarly priced ultraportables from other Windows manufacturers, the touch display and 120Hz refresh rate are still not standard features at this price. Plenty of rivals still ship 60Hz non-touch panels as the default, reserving touch and high refresh rates for pricier configurations. The XPS 13 includes both from the base model.

It's a fair comparison to make against the MacBook Neo too, since many buyers considering a Windows laptop under $1,000 are also considering Apple's entry point. The two take genuinely different approaches. MacBook Neo has the edge in starting price and offers straightforward access to Apple's ecosystem and Apple Intelligence. The XPS 13 answers with a touchscreen, a backlit keyboard, a 120Hz display, and memory that isn't hard-capped, none of which the entry-level MacBook Neo offers. The Neo ships with a fixed 8GB of memory and no option to configure higher, while the XPS 13 can be stepped up to 16GB. Neither laptop is a strictly better choice than the other. It comes down to whether touch, a higher refresh rate, and configurability matter more to you than staying inside Apple's ecosystem at the lowest possible price.

What you're arguably giving up

It would be misleading to write about the XPS 13 without being honest about its limits, and port availability is the biggest one. The laptop has two USB-C ports and nothing else: no card reader and no dedicated USB-A. That's the same port count as most ultraportable rivals at this size, so it's not unusually restrictive, but those relying on older peripherals will want a dongle or a dock on hand.

It's also worth being clear that the XPS 13 isn't a Copilot+ PC (although it will be with the forthcoming PTL launch). That designation, and the on-device AI features that come with it, sit with Dell's XPS 14 and a handful of other models in the range. If Copilot+ features are a priority, the XPS 13 isn't the model to consider.

Neither of these are a deal-breaker for the audience this laptop is built for, but they're the honest reasons someone might choose a different laptop, even one at a similar price.

A genuine option for students

Credit: Dell

Dell is also offering the XPS 13 to students at $599 (available on the DX13260 model only), through November 2. That's a meaningful discount on top of an already competitive starting price, and it puts a laptop with this build quality and screen within reach of a college budget. Anyone eligible should factor the expiry date into their decision, since the offer isn't ongoing.

Who the Dell XPS 13 laptop makes sense for

The XPS 13 is best suited to buyers who want a laptop that feels premium without stretching into four-figure territory. Students, remote workers, and those whose daily computing revolves around browsing, writing, video calls, and streaming will get the most out of it. If your work leans more into heavy multitasking, video editing, or anything that benefits from more memory and a wider array of ports, it's worth looking further up Dell's range, where models like the Dell 14S offer more connectivity, or the XPS 14 offers more memory headroom and Copilot+ support.

For most people shopping specifically in the under $1,000 Windows laptop category, though, the XPS 13 does more for the price than almost anything else currently available. It's not trying to be the fastest or most feature-complete laptop on the market. It's making a simpler case: a genuinely good screen, a build quality that doesn't feel like a compromise, and a battery that lasts, all for less than four figures. That's a hard combination to find, and it's the reason the XPS 13 belongs near the top of any list built around this budget.

item.title: I priced out a PS5 Pro equivalent gaming PC and walked away with the console instead
item.itunes:title: I priced out a PS5 Pro equivalent gaming PC and walked away with the console instead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A few years ago, building a gaming PC equivalent to the PS5 Pro didn't seem particularly difficult. GPUs like the 16GB AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT were readily available at somewhat reasonable launch prices, and building a system that could go head-to-head with the PlayStation 5 Pro wouldn't cost a fortune.

With GPU prices climbing well beyond their launch MSRPs, and RAM and SSD prices surging, the same can't be said now. So while I initially wanted to build a gaming PC to beat the PlayStation 5 Pro, pricing out the components made me less sure about the decision.

Building a PS5 Pro-equivalent gaming PC is more expensive than I expected

Even with the recent PlayStation 5 Pro price hike, the console wins

As with any other build, I started planning around the graphics card; for reference, the PS5 Pro GPU's performance is roughly comparable to the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB or the Radeon RX 9060 XT. Among these two, Nvidia launched the former with an initial MSRP of $429, while the 16GB AMD GPU launched at $349.

The current pricing, on the other hand, is much higher for both GPUs. It's hard to find the 16GB RTX 5060 Ti under $800, even with discounts, and the Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB rarely falls below $500.

An 8GB GPU would have saved me some money, but since I'm targeting 4K gaming, like the PS5 Pro, 16GB of VRAM was a core requirement.

GPU prices are awful, and integrated graphics are saving budget PCs

Modern iGPUs are making budget gaming PCs more viable.

By  Abid Ahsan Shanto

The rest of the components didn't make things any easier

Current RAM and SSD prices make the build even harder to justify

Even if I managed to secure the GPU for under $400 by scouring the second-hand market, it would still be hard to match the PS5 Pro's performance at its current retail price of $899.99. The reason is that the RAM and SSD prices have climbed sharply as well.

A decent 16GB DDR5 kit would have cost under $100 in mid to late 2025, but now it costs over $200. SSD prices have followed a similar trend, with good 1TB drives now costing over $150, even on sale.

Lexar NM790 1TB SSD

The Lexar NM790 1TB SSD offers super-fast Gen4 speeds, is compatible with the PS5, comes with a heatsink, and doesn't cost a lot.

See at Amazon

These hiked prices for RAM and SSDs quickly add up when combined with the rest of the hardware. A Ryzen 5 7600X with a relatively good B650 motherboard and a decent power supply would cost around $500 in total.

With 16GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD added, the total is over $900, and with the GPU included, the total easily reaches around $1,500. The PS5 Pro, on the other hand, retails for $899.99, making it 40% cheaper than an equivalent PC build.

Getting Linux onto a PS5 screeches to a halt after the hypervisor bug it relies on was reported to Sony

All good things must come to an end.

2
By  Simon Batt

Even Valve couldn't make a console-like PC cheaper

The Steam Machine shows just how expensive PC hardware has become

Credit: Valve

My part list isn't really the most convincing part of this comparison. Valve also tried to package PC hardware into a console-like gaming machine, and while there were hopes at the beginning, it ended up being more costly than the PlayStation 5 Pro.

For reference, despite having relatively less capable hardware, the Steam Machine starts at $1,049 and doesn't even include a bundled controller. Of course, even with the PS5 Pro being cheaper than a comparable PC or the Steam Machine, it's not the better overall platform.

The Steam Machine, for instance, has the flexibility of a PC, while Sony locks the PS5 Pro into its own ecosystem. Even so, putting PC hardware into a console-sized gaming system doesn't make the economics work in its favor.

I called the Steam Machine overpriced in July, and now it's the cheapest PC I'd actually buy

The best deal you can get right now... is the Steam Machine?

2
By  Abhinav Raj

PS5 Pro has the optimization advantage that a PC can't replicate

Developers know exactly what hardware they are targeting

The win for the PS5 Pro goes beyond the part list and the cost associated with it. Developers know exactly what every console owner has, giving them a fixed target when optimizing games. On PC, even two systems with the same GPU can run the same game differently, so developers must consider a wide range of configurations to optimize a game.

Of course, this doesn't automatically mean that the PS5 Pro will outperform a powerful gaming PC. A performance-focused build can push higher settings, better ray tracing, and higher frame rates, but it would require high-end components.

It took one weekend to make my gaming PC dramatically quieter without spending a penny

My PC's quieter and my wallet isn't lighter

By  Samarveer Singh

I bought the PS5 Pro instead

The PC still wins on flexibility, but the math no longer works for me

I started pricing out components, thinking a powerful gaming PC would be the obvious choice, but the total cost made me choose the PS5 Pro instead. I would be giving up flexibility, a large free games collection, and better upgradability.

It's worth noting that the PlayStation 5 Pro isn't suddenly a bargain, but today's component prices have made it easier to justify. If market conditions were different, I would probably lean more toward the gaming PC, as I initially did.

PC gaming is becoming a luxury: Why the RAM crisis is a win for consoles

Every day now, a new PS5 or Xbox makes undeniably more sense.

item.title: I play my PS2 collection upscaled to 4K, and some of the games look like remasters
item.itunes:title: I play my PS2 collection upscaled to 4K, and some of the games look like remasters
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When the PlayStation 2 came out, I wasn't even born yet. But as a child, I got to experience an era when it peaked in popularity, and everyone at school knew it was the one gaming console you had to have. Some of the classics from that time truly set the stage for the modern gaming industry with vast open worlds, cinematic storytelling, and design choices that still influence what we play today.

I've found myself revisiting that library quite often, of course, not without the help of a few modern conveniences. After a few evenings with one of my favorite titles, I'd say there's no better way to revisit the classics than in 4K. All it took was an emulator, a little configuration, and a streaming app to send the feed to the TV.

The setup is an emulator and an open-source streaming app

PCSX2 does the upscaling, and Sunshine and Moonlight handle the streaming

If you're looking to emulate PS2 games on PC, you don't need to go beyond PCSX2. That's true if you're trying to upscale them, too, because the emulator can handle it. PCSX2 can take a PS2 game's 480p output and render it at 2x, 3x, 4x, or even 8x the console's native resolution, which gets you comfortably beyond 4K.

For most games, though, the sweet spot is often between 3x and 4x without running into issues or artifacts with UI elements, shadows, or sprites, as I did on my setup with a Ryzen 5 7600X and an RTX 4070 Ti Super.

I rely on the Sunshine/Moonlight duo to get that feed onto the TV. Sunshine runs on my PC and captures the PCSX2 output before encoding it, while Moonlight on my Google TV receives the stream over my home network.

The Prince of Persia: Sands of Time remake got canceled, so I made my own in 4K

The emulator almost does what Ubisoft couldn't in six years

item.title: 4 things I 3D printed for my PC that work better than anything I could buy
item.itunes:title: 4 things I 3D printed for my PC that work better than anything I could buy
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
3D printing has come a long way in the last few years and has enabled people to go from having it as a hobby to printing parts that both look good and are functional. Personally, when I started, it was more about learning the hobby and designing parts, but my printer has earned its keep by helping me fix small annoyances around my house and my workspace. Sure, you can probably buy things online from Amazon, but with 3D printing you have the ability to customize parts to your liking and to suit your needs.

GPU anti-sag holder

GPUs are getting beefier, and it's always better to add extra support

There are multiple companies that currently sell GPU anti-sag brackets with most costing between $20–50. However, with a 3D printer it's quite easy to print one for cheap and, with the right color, it can complement your setup as well. I recently printed one for my 3080Ti Founders Edition that had started to sag quite a bit lately. The print used a few grams of filament and was able to print quickly, not to mention it goes well with my setup. There is also a multicolor version of this print with Nvidia or Radeon branding, giving you additional customization options.

3.5-inch drive holder

A drive cage for my 3.5-inch HDDs so they can be stored safely

The explosion of AI has been driving prices of all PC hardware, including storage, and may tempt some to start using HDDs again, especially for storing content that is not required to be accessed every day. I had a few old drives that were not in use and I decided to move media files, like photos and videos that I don't normally access every day from my SSD to HDD. I found a great model online that can hold three 3.5-inch HDDs in a rack with their ports exposed so you can directly wire the drives into your system and use them. This also works well if you have a mini-PC that you were planning to convert into a NAS but do not have enough space to put all the drives inside.

Bonus: There is also a similar model for a 2.5-inch SSD/HDDs if you have a smaller form factor drive and are looking for a way to store them or set them up for a NAS or a server.

6 small 3D-printed parts that make PC building easier

Tired of PC building frustrations? These small 3D-printed solutions will revolutionize your setup.

By  Jeff Butts

3D printed cable management ties

Custom-sized ties for odd cable runs

Cable management ties are perfect for hiding away those pesky wires. The problem is I never have enough of them or size is an issue when trying to bundle up a bunch of cables. Thankfully, 3D printed ties are just as good and cost a few cents to a dollar to print. There are multiple models online that you can use to print cable management ties and the good thing is that you can size them to get the perfect length. 3D printing cable management ties also means that you will never run out of them mid-build or when you finally decide to tuck away those hanging cables under your desk.

Cable management ties need to be flexible in order to work well. Using generic PLA may not be the best approach as PLA is usually brittle and can break when trying to bend the cable management tie. I had limited luck with using PETG that has been properly dried instead of PLA. The best, of course, would be TPU because of its flexibility. However, not all printers can print TPU, so PETG is a better middle-of-the-ground option. You can, however, use PETG to print zip ties instead.

Fan dust filters

Dust-less PC is a healthy PC

Dust is one of the biggest reasons why PCs get louder and underperform over time. While most manufacturers do provide a basic dust filter with a PC case, you can also 3D print it for cheap that may suit your build aesthetic while being functional as well. There are multiple models across different websites like Printables, where you can get models for dust filters and printing them will not cost you more than a few dollars. You can print fans in PLA, which is the most widely used filament for 3D printing, but I personally printed a couple of mine in PETG for better overall strength and higher temperature resistance.

If you are looking for something fancier, there are also custom fan grill models that can further add to the overall look and feel of your build while ensuring that you have enough and more airflow. These don't add much in terms of functionality to your build but cost a few dollars to print and can give more personality to your setup.

PLA and PETG win at different jobs, and matching the material to the part saved me hundreds in failed prints

PLA prints fine details, but PETG is the only material that survives actual use

1
By  Ayush Pande

Print the fix before you buy the part

None of the prints here are rocket science or cleaver, but they work well and cost a few dollars to print. Each of these can be found on the market as well, but they won't be customized to your liking or size. That's where 3D printed models shine as they give more control over the color, design, and the size of the part that you are looking for to complete your build. The 3D printing community usually provides a bunch of innovative models that can address your needs without breaking the bank for customization.
